analysis.investment_thesis: Campus is a recognisable mass-market sports footwear brand with genuinely good return ratios (ROE 29.5%, ROCE 31.8%), but at 55.7x P/E the market is pricing in perfection for a business that delivered flat revenue between FY23–FY24 and wildly volatile profits (₹27 Cr → ₹108 Cr → ₹89 Cr → ₹121 Cr). I will not pay a premium price for an inconsistent business — that is how permanent capital loss happens.
key_strengths: Strong return ratios — ROE 29.5% and ROCE 31.8% show the underlying asset-light brand economics are real
Improving free cash flow — FCF turned solidly positive at ₹219 Cr (FY24) and ₹176 Cr (FY25) after years of erratic generation
Promoter holding at 72% with no visible selling — skin in the game is adequate
key_risks: Valuation is prohibitive — P/E 55.7x and EV/EBITDA 33x for a footwear brand with stagnant FY23–FY24 revenue; I need 12–20x for quality
D/E of 0.48 is just below my hard limit of 0.5 — unacceptable headroom in a cyclical consumer discretionary segment
Earnings chronically volatile — net profit swung from ₹27 Cr (FY21) to ₹108 Cr (FY22) to ₹89 Cr (FY24); no predictability, which I find disqualifying
red_flags: Revenue growth has stalled: ₹1,484 Cr (FY23) → ₹1,448 Cr (FY24) → ₹1,593 Cr (FY25) — barely 3-year CAGR of ~3.5%, far below my 10–15% requirement
D/E at 0.48 breaches my comfort zone of <0.3; for a consumer discretionary brand this leverage is unnecessary and dangerous
Operating income fell sharply from ₹242 Cr (FY22) to ₹143 Cr (FY24) despite higher revenue — margin erosion signals weak pricing power or cost discipline problems
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Campus has built a credible brand in the ₹500–1,500 price-point sports footwear segment — a space I respect because it serves the broad Indian middle class. The return ratios are genuinely impressive, and the shift to positive free cash flow in FY24–FY25 is encouraging. However, the business has repeatedly failed to grow steadily: revenue was essentially flat between FY23 and FY24, operating income declined from ₹242 Cr in FY22 to ₹143 Cr in FY24, and net profit has yo-yoed around with no discernible upward trend. This is not the quiet compounder I look for — it is a cyclical brand story with lumpy execution.

The valuation makes the case impossible for me. At 55.7x trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA of 33x, the market is pricing in a high-quality, high-growth consumer franchise. But the actual growth numbers — ~10% revenue CAGR over the last 3 years, stagnant in absolute terms — do not justify that multiple. I built DMart by paying fair prices for businesses I understood deeply. Paying 55x earnings for a footwear brand that also carries D/E of 0.48 is speculation, not investing. I would revisit if the price fell to ₹80–100 range (implying ~20x P/E) and if debt were eliminated.
